planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer or early fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, giving the bed a summer-dry rest once foliage yellows.

directions: Helen's fawn lily is a California native trout lily found on serpentine and clay soils in open oak woodland and chaparral margins of the North Coast Ranges, where it blooms from late winter into early spring. Each stem carries one to several nodding white flowers with a yellow basal zone above mottled, glossy green leaves, forming loose colonies that go fully dormant by early summer as the surrounding woodland dries out. Plant corms where winter and spring moisture are followed by a dry summer rest, such as a raised bed or slope under deciduous oaks, rather than in a consistently damp border. Because wild populations are localized, only source nursery-propagated corms rather than wild-collected material.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer or early fall in sharply drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade on a slope that stays dry in summer.

directions: Native to the Illinois Valley of southwest Oregon, Howell's fawn lily grows on serpentine-influenced soils in open oak and conifer woodland, where it is closely related to and sometimes confused with the showier Henderson's fawn lily. Mottled leaves emerge in late winter followed by nodding, pale lavender-pink flowers with a yellow throat, carried singly or a few per stem in early spring before the plant retreats underground for its long summer dormancy. It wants the same wet-winter, dry-summer rhythm as other western Erythronium species, so plant it in a rock garden or raised bed with excellent drainage rather than a moist eastern-style woodland border. Because its native range is narrow and serpentine-restricted, buy only nursery-propagated corms.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath conifers, mimicking its high-elevation forest-edge habitat.

directions: Klamath fawn lily is a small, high-elevation trout lily of the Klamath-Siskiyou Mountains of northern California and southern Oregon, growing in coniferous forest openings and wet mountain meadow margins where snowmelt keeps soil moist into spring. Slender, mostly unmottled leaves give rise to a single small white flower with a yellow base on each stem, blooming as snow retreats and finished well before the forest canopy fully closes for summer. Because it comes from cool, high-elevation sites, it appreciates a shadier, more consistently moist spot than lowland California Erythronium species and resents prolonged summer heat. Best suited to woodland gardens in cooler climates or a shaded, humus-rich bed that does not bake dry in summer.

planting.note: Plant small tubers in early spring in cool, gritty, humus-rich soil that never dries out, in partial to full shade protected from hot afternoon sun.

directions: Kashmir corydalis is a small Himalayan woodland and alpine-margin species prized for flowers of an unusually pure, electric blue, carried in short racemes above finely divided, ferny foliage in late spring. It is notoriously intolerant of heat and drought, thriving only where summers stay cool and the soil remains evenly moist, which makes it best suited to climates with mild summers or to a shaded, well-ventilated spot such as a north-facing rock garden pocket. Unlike the more heat-tolerant yellow Corydalis species, this one resents both soggy winter soil and summer baking, so gritty, humus-rich drainage paired with consistent moisture is essential. Gardeners outside cool-summer regions often grow it in a shaded alpine bed or trough where conditions can be more closely controlled.

planting.note: Divide and plant rhizome sections in fall in moist, humus-rich, neutral to alkaline woodland soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Nine-leaved toothwort is a European woodland spring ephemeral found carpeting beech and mixed deciduous forests from the Alps through central and southern Europe, where its whorl of three ternate leaves gives the plant its species name. Nodding, pale cream to soft yellow four-petaled flowers open in short clusters in early to mid spring just as the leaves unfurl, then the whole plant withers back underground by early summer as the forest canopy closes overhead. It spreads gradually by shallow, scaly rhizomes to form loose patches and is best left undisturbed once established, since it resents being moved while in active growth. Use it as an early-season companion to later-emerging ferns and hostas in a shaded, humus-rich woodland bed.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in partial shade at a woodland edge, where winter-spring moisture is followed by a dry summer rest.

directions: Greek fritillary grows wild in open woodland, scrub, and rocky hillsides across Greece and the southern Balkans, where it flowers in early spring before the surrounding shrub and tree canopy fully leafs out. Slender stems carry one or two nodding, bell-shaped flowers in muted green, bronze, or maroon tones, often faintly checkered, above a few narrow grey-green leaves, giving it a quieter presence than the showier checkered fritillary. It wants sharp drainage and a dry summer dormancy in the manner of other Mediterranean woodland-margin bulbs, so a partially shaded raised bed or slope under deciduous shrubs suits it better than a consistently damp border. Grow it among dry-shade companions that tolerate summer baking once the fritillary's foliage has died back.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade under deciduous trees or shrubs.

directions: Italian bluebell is native to woodland and scrub margins of northwestern Italy and southeastern France, where it is the earliest-blooming of the bluebell group, opening in early spring ahead of the Spanish and English bluebells. Its flowers are held in a tight, conical raceme rather than a one-sided arching spike, each small star-shaped bloom a clear mid-blue with a faint fragrance, above narrow, glossy, strap-like leaves. More compact and sun-tolerant than its woodland relatives, it still performs best with the dappled light of a high deciduous canopy and soil that stays humus-rich without waterlogging. Plant in drifts at a woodland edge or in a shaded border where its earlier bloom extends the bluebell season before the larger-growing species take over.
